prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and its realization at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B024 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. The test I apply is whether we can name the original idea, the original experiment and independent verification. Katori proposed trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the lattice does not shift the clock transition, and he realized the first strontium lattice clock. Ye's group then showed what the concept could do, taking uncertainty and stability to the 1e-18 level and making the first controlled study of interactions inside a lattice clock. JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE now reproduce this in Sr, Yb and Hg, and the clocks are compared across continents. The consequences are measured rather than promised: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tighter limits on drifting constants, and a new regime of many-body physics in a clock. The chair asked whether this is distinct from 2005 and 2012. I think it is. The comb made optical frequencies countable, and ion control showed single-quantum-system clocks. Neither contains the idea of interrogating thousands of neutral atoms in a perturbation-free lattice. I would therefore write the citation on the invention and its realization, and not on the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains overlap with the lineage already recognized in 2005 and 2012, and the fact that a clock is an instrument we built, not a phenomenon nature surprised us with. I do not find that decisive, since the committee has often rewarded tools that open a door, but I accept that it is the main reason B003 deserves a hearing. The second objection is credit. Lemonde (SYRTE), Takamoto and Ludlow all made milestone demonstrations that a two-name credit passes over. My reading of the record is that the invention belongs to Katori, that the first Sr lattice-clock operation and the record accuracy and many-body work belong to Katori and Ye, and that the others built on or independently confirmed a scheme that had already been proposed. That is a judgment about priority, not a certainty, and I would want the secretariat's historical check on the dates of the first demonstrations before the final vote.

responses.point: Kroll and Lindroth want the many-body and interaction physics inside the clock considered in the B024 case, and Kroll asks whether Ye's record-accuracy work is invention or engineering and systematics control.
responses.response: The question matters because it decides whether Ye belongs in the credit at all. I would not call his contribution routine systematics control. Controlling lattice-clock shifts and the first quantitative study of collisional and many-body effects were original experimental results, and they are what turned Katori's proposal into a clock that others could copy. I would keep the citation anchored on the invention and the realization, but I would let the word realization cover Ye's demonstration of the 1e-18 regime, and I would leave the many-body physics as a consequence and not name it. A longer citation would invite the very priority arguments we are trying to avoid.

responses.point: Lindroth places Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley as important only for specific milestones and asks that the case not depend on the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree on both points and I am glad that you, as the atomic physics voice, are explicit that the claims of Lemonde and Ludlow are milestone claims. That is the answer to the chair's first question as I read it. Lemonde's group worked in parallel on the same lattice idea, but the proposal and first realization are Katori's. I stay concerned about Takamoto, who is a member of the original RIKEN work, and I would only accept the two-name credit if the first-demonstration chronology confirms this. I also agree with leaving the redefinition out of the text, since the criterion is what has been demonstrated.

responses.point: Danielsson argues for B003 as a discovery with the pattern of prediction, surprise and wide replication, and says an unsettled superconducting mechanism has not blocked earlier prizes.
responses.response: That is a fair historical point and I do not hold the open mechanism against B003 as a matter of principle. Where I still differ is on credit. The 2018 experimental breakthrough is associated with Cao and his colleagues, and a prize naming MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer would honour the prediction and the group leader while leaving out the person who made the original observation. I am not sure we can say we have identified the people who did the original experiment. Other groups are still bringing out the field, and with one or two more years of consolidation the picture should be clearer. I appreciate that you would be content to see B024 first, and I regard B003 as the strongest next candidate.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers active matter (B006) and lists B003 and B023, not B024, among his alternatives, while saying he would not seriously oppose colleagues on B024.
responses.response: I take your non-opposition seriously, and I share your reservation on B006: the question Johansson and Lindroth put is the right one. I cannot point to a quantitative experimental test of the Toner-Tu exponents that I would regard as an original, verified result of the kind the prize requires, and as an experimentalist I need that before supporting it. Your view that B024 is a refinement is the main scientific dispute on the table. My answer is that the committee asks for an invention that opens a new regime, and a lattice holding thousands of neutral atoms without trap shifts, with the resulting stabilities, is that. I do not see that it is a continuation of the comb.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks that the first demonstrations be checked and that the citation not rely on the pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I support both requests and accept the first as a condition. On the second, my citation says nothing about the SI second. I would go further: if the chronology shows that Takamoto's 2005 demonstration was an independent first operation rather than part of Katori's own program, I would want to see the committee discuss it explicitly, and I would be ready to reconsider only if a clear alternative credit emerged within the three-name limit.

uncertainties: Whether the secretariat's check on the first Sr lattice-clock demonstrations supports a two-name credit that passes over Takamoto, Lemonde and Ludlow.
Whether the committee will treat the clock as an invention distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether a combined or two-part configuration with B003 would draw explicit support, since the credited names would exceed three people.
Whether B003 will be mature, with the pairing mechanism and the credit for Cao clearer, in one to three years.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I am an electron microscopist who works with aberration-corrected instruments, so I proposed B001 and ranked it first, and I have kept it only as an alternative and will not promote or vote for it as a lead. I have no collaboration or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, and no conflict on B024 or B003. Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, but that has no bearing on B024.
